# Kiṁpakkajātaka (Ja 85)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kiṁpakkajātaka* (Ja 85) is a short narrative belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [Fausböll 1877]. Set at Jetavana, the introductory story relates that the Buddha addressed a monk who was troubled by lustful longing (*ukkanṭhita*) after seeing an elaborately adorned woman during his almsround in Sāvatthī [Fausböll 1877]. Opening with the verse incipit *Āyatiṁ dosaṁ nāññāya*, the Buddha relates a past life in which he was a caravan leader (*satthavāho*) [Fausböll 1877]. In that past existence, members of his caravan ignored his warnings and consumed the sweet, fragrant fruit of the *kimpakka* tree—mistaking its appearance, boughs, and taste for those of a mango tree—which resulted in their severe poisoning and death [Deleanu 2006; Lamotte; Fausböll 1877].

 However, Étienne Lamotte cites the Jātaka in comparative annotation to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra* when discussing analogous Indian folktales of poisonous or wondrous fruits [Lamotte].

- [Fausböll 1877] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 1 (1877) — Provided the Pali edition, verse incipit, setting at Jetavana, and the Bodhisatta's role as caravan leader.
- [Lamotte] Étienne Lamotte, Le Traité de la Grande Vertu de Sagesse de Nāgārjuna (Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra), Vol. 2 — Noted the story of the caravan eating kimpaka fruit mistaken for mangoes in comparison with the Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra.
